ety.text: First attested in 1541 as labdomen. Borrowed from Middle French abdomen as well as from its etymon Latin abdōmen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + -dō (“put, place”).

senses.d: The belly, or that part of the body between the thorax and the pelvis, not including the back; or in some lower vertebrates, the portion between the cardiac and caudal regions.

The cavity of the belly, which is lined by the peritoneum, and contains the viscera; often restricted in humans to the part between the diaphragm and the commencement of the pelvis, the remainder being called the pelvic cavity.
ex: He was all bent over complaining of pains in the abdomen.

senses.d: The posterior section of the body, behind the thorax, in insects, crustaceans, and other Arthropoda.

grp.label: posterior section of an arthropod's body

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish vientre, from Latin ventrem (“stomach, belly”), from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.

pt:abdômen.gl: Brazilian Portuguese standard spelling of abdómen

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin abdomen (“belly, abdomen”).
First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the abdomen; ventral.
Characterized by or possessing a large abdomen; corpulent, pot-bellied.
ex: The moment they had passed, the pikes clashed together horizontally to bar the gateway, and all but pinned an abdominal citizen that sought to wedge in along with them.

senses.d: Having the ventral fins under the abdomen and behind the pectoral fins.
Belonging to the order Abdominales of fish.
A fish of the order Abdominales.

grp.label: of or pertaining to the abdomen

ety.text: From New Latin abdōminālis (“abdominal”). By surface analysis, addome (“abdomen”) + -in- + -ale.
